speechtext:
Would you like
it, though?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Well, I do not need a
couple of glasses of .whiskey anyway. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) in the course of his speech yesterday commented upon the amendment and said he did not agree with it. Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to say to him that we in this quarter of the House will uphold him in everything else he said yesterday. He asked that the tariff board have a Hansard report of its proceedings. He asked that all the information given to that board be laid before every member of this House. When my friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked the hon. Minister of Finance for reports of the evidence that was given-not only copies of the briefs submitted by the manufacturers who wanted more protection, but reports of all the evidence submitted for and against their applications, the minister said that it would be too costly to have the proceedings reported fully, and that if my hon. friend wanted certain evidence he would have to ask for it specially. That is not the position we take. That is not the position the hon. member for Weyburn takes. He urges that this House should decide tariff questions and should be in possession of all the evidence upon which the tariff board bases its recommendations. I support my hon. friend in that request, and I hope he will have sufficient influence with his party so that the members of this House and the country at large may know exactly what goes on before the tariff board by being supplied with a Hansard report of all the evidence upon which that board bases its recommendations.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I have been present at several sittings of the tariff board, and I want to say that no gentleman was more carefully prepared and more thoroughly looked after the interests of the consumers of this country than the hon. member for Wey-bum, absolutely to his own loss. Unlike the boot manufacturers for instance, he was not concerned in the few thousand people

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
that make shoes; he was interested in the nine million people that wear those shoes. I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that the suggestion of my hon. friend from Weyburn ought to be put into effect, and I can assure him that he will receive all the help we are capable of to that end.
Mr. H. C. HOCIvEN (Toronto West Centre):	Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend who
has just taken his seat (Mr. Adshead) says you cannot inn with the hare and hunt with the hounds. If he sits in this House for any length of time he will discover that that is quite possible, because the government of the day is running with the free trade hare and hunting with the protectionist hounds of Quebec. My hon. friend is surprised that a man should get up on that side of the House and say he is a protectionist. It gives him a shock. Why, Sir, we have had members from all parts of Quebec stand in their places and over and over again declare themselves protectionists. We had a member from that province condemn the Prime Minister, his leader, because he reduced the tariff duties on that celebrated occasion which was "the first crack out of the box." Mr. Marler stood in his place representing a constituency in Quebec

speechtext:
He is now replaced by a
rather superior man. He stated on the floor of the House that he had been authorized by the leaders of his party to go to the manufacturers of Quebec and tell them that the tariff would not be reduced, notwithstanding the free trade clause in the platform of 1919. AVell, the tariff was reduced afterwards because the free trade hares had-

speechtext: Scared the hounds.

speechtext: -a little more influence with the government than the protectionists, and the government stood up most bravely and declared they were going to reduce tariff duties. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said "This is the death-knell of protection". My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) said, "This is the first crack out of the box". There was loud applause from our Progressive friends all of whom were then on this side of the House. But that was the only time it ever was done. The government discovered that that policy was not going to get them support in the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
The hounds caught up
with the hares.

speechtext:
Yes. The death-knell of
protection was not sounded. My hon. friend
need not be surprised if he finds men getting up on that side of the House and declaring themselves for protection. Quebec needs protection as much as any part of the Dominion -perhaps a little more-and she is not going to submit to any radical reduction in duties. True, Quebec did consent most cheerfully to the reduction in the automobile duties because her manufacturers do not make automobiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: They do not want to.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend presume to be the spokesman of Quebec?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I have been charged with a great many things but I hope Providence will preserve me from that. I want to tell my hon. friend from East Calgary what the truth is about the automobile duty. The duty was reduced but the sales tax was taken off and other advantages were given to the automobile industry that left it as fully protected as before the duty was reduced. That is the fact.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Did not automobiles cost less to the consumer?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: The reduction materially affected the revenues of the country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Did it not affect the purchaser?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: It affected the revenues of the country, which is pretty much the same thing.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend the
figures from the Bureau of Statistics to show in what way the revenues were affected?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not think we need to get the statistics to prove this fact, that if there is a sales tax of five per cent on a certain article

which five per cent goes into the coffers of the country-if that sales tax is removed, that much revenue is cut off. The reduction in the sales tax to that extent necessarily means a reduction in the revenue.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that the revenue from passenger cars was $570,000 greater in the period of nine months ending in January than it was the year before?

speechtext: I am talking about the sales tax; my hon. friend is talking about the volume of trade.

speechtext:
I did get twisted on the
sales tax and the excise tax, but there are so many taxes under this government that it is pretty hard to keep track of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: These taxes were imposed by the previous government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from East Calgary is very much opposed to the reduction of the income tax. We had some figures given to us recently which would make it quite reasonable to understand this opposition. The west does not pay any income tax that is worth while. The two provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta pay $2,317,000 in income tax and this amount is all paid by the cities. On the other hand, the province of Ontario paid last year $26,539,000 in income tax and the province of Quebec, in round figures, $18,000,000. So that these two central provinces pay the vast bulk of the tax, and it is noit to be wondered at that my hon. friend should want to have the tax maintained. The farmers of Saskatchewan and Alberta who pay no income tax naturally say, " Certainly, let us soak the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and make them pay the revenues of the country." There is therefore no reason why my hon. friend should rejoice particularly in any reduction of the income tax.
